new_entities.name: Sleep extension in adolescents
new_entities.description: Interventions that deliberately increase sleep opportunity or sleep duration in adolescents.

new_entities.name: Academic performance
new_entities.description: Academic functioning such as classroom attention, quiz performance, and school-related performance.

edges.effect_quant: A randomized simulated-classroom study found that adolescents performed better on lecture-based quizzes and showed better classroom attention after healthy sleep than after multi-night sleep restriction, while a 2025 in-home crossover sleep-extension trial increased sleep duration by 1.37 hours and supports the causal plausibility of school-night sleep extension as a performance-relevant intervention.
edges.population: adolescents with insufficient sleep or experimentally manipulated sleep schedules
edges.mechanism: Additional sleep improves alertness, sustained attention, and learning efficiency, which can translate into better classroom engagement and academic task performance.
edges.summary: Sleep extension has a real protective signal for school-related functioning in adolescents. The evidence base is still modest, but controlled studies support the view that increasing sleep opportunity improves performance-relevant outcomes rather than merely correlating with them.
edges.caveats: Most intervention trials rely on short-term or simulated academic measures rather than long-term grade outcomes. Benefits should be framed as improvements in learning readiness and classroom performance, not guaranteed grade inflation.

evidence.notes: Impact of Multi-Night Experimentally Induced Short Sleep on Adolescent Performance in a Simulated Classroom.
Changes in circadian timing following a 1-week in-home sleep extension manipulation in habitually short-sleeping adolescents.

evidence.citation: Kira G et al 2014 J Clin Sleep Med
